Don't get me wrong, I'm a big fan of letting the free market determine prices by means of supply and demand, but some products/industries don't actually work that way.

You'll get inelastic demand whenever you have a product which is rarely needed, but is still necessary.

For instance, let's say there is a rare and fatal disease. Only 1 out of 1,000,000 people contract this disease each year and any random person in the population can contract this disease. HOWEVER, there is a cure for this disease. But, that cure cost a fuck-ton of money to research and develop.

That cure will never go to market because the demand is inelastic. A drug company can't distribute a cure for a handful of people each year without selling it for an extreme amount of money. So much money that the people depending on the cure can't even pay for it.

The solution to inelastic demand is to distribute the burden to everyone, since everyone is randomly as likely to get the disease as anyone else.

Another example is when a technology is so cutting edge that no-one can possibly buy it and so no company is going to pay to develop it.

For instance, the Computer. For nearly 100 years, Babbage's Difference Engine was just a curiosity for mathematicians. But, no company would seriously consider building one because it was insanely expensive and nobody was buying. Finally WWII happens and the government realizes this silly toy might be useful to decrypt Nazi messages.

So the government lowers the barrier to entry doing all the R&D and companies like AT&T and IBM can use that R&D to produce computers at a lower cost and because the cost is lowered to a reasonable price, now there can exist a market. But during the R&D phase, it was an inelastic market. There was 1 customer, the government.

Same can be said of the Internet. During the R&D phase, the market for the internet was inelastic. Nobody owned a computer apart from the government and a handful of universities. There's no way an ISP could have survived that kind of market. Too few customers, too high R&D costs.

The difference between these examples and yours is, EVERYONE needs police, EVERYONE needs utilities, EVERYONE needs trash pickup. A private company could potentially take these needs and market them. But imagine you live in a town with only 5 houses, no company is going to bother. They just can't make a profit off of 5 houses.
